## Summary

### Dry Bite

80-90%

### Rate of Envenoming

10-20%

### Venomous

Moderate Risk

Severe envenoming possible, potentially lethal

## Antivenom

### Antivenom Therapy

Antivenom is the key treatment for systemic envenoming. Multiple doses may be required.

### Antivenom Dosage

Refer to dosage schedule for relevant antivenoms listed on this site

### Antivenom Reactions

Full range possible; see relevant section in antivenom pages

### Adverse Antivenom Reaction Management

Cease antivenom, resuscitate, adrenaline, IV fluids, then cautiously restart antivenom

### Known Antivenoms
#### NOTE: Order of antivenoms is not indicitive of preference.

Funnel-web spider antivenom

IAuCSL04 by CSL
#### Description

Lyophilized powder plus diluent

#### Comments

#### Recommended Dose

2 vials, or 4 vials if severe envenoming is evident. Further doses may be required in very severe cases, or if there is relapse of envenoming.

#### Source Species

Atrax robustus ( males ). Specimens from Gosford area of New South Wales.

#### Coverage Species

Atrax robustus , other Atrax species , Hadronyche species. There is evidence this antivenom is also effective against Missulena spp. venom, but bites by these spiders rarely require antivenom treatment.

#### Storage Type

Freeze dried antivenom. Does not require refrigeration but should not be stored in high temperature environments. Acceptable (and common practice) to store in a refrigerator, along with other antivenoms which do require refrigeration.

#### type

Spider (SP)

#### Status

In production

#### Immunisation Host

Horse serum

#### Administration Route

i.v.

#### Volume

6.2 ml ( approx. )

#### Initial Dose

2 vials

#### Local Cost

AUD $1008.46 ex GST (2011).

#### Storage Life

3 years, Expiry date on label.

#### Language on Label

English

## Case Studies

Browne G.J. (1997) Near fatal envenomation from the funnel-web spider in an infant. Pediatr. Emerg. Care, Vol. 13, No. 4, pp 271-273.

Case Report.
9 month old baby girl , playing on floor of laundry at home. Baby noted to scream, mother saw baby clutching a large black spider in (R) hand. Mother (a Registered nurse) quickly applied a pressure immobilization bandage with a limb splint and trapped the spider - subsequently identified as
Atrax robustus. Several bites had been noted on child's hand. Soon after baby was sweating; drooling; salivating and had stridor.
On arrival at hospital , 25 min. post bite - pallid; unresponsive; respirations - 60 per min; appeared dyspnoeic; blood [pressure - 127/ 104 mm.Hg; pulse - 200 b.p.m. Appeared generally flushed. Subsequently deteriorated rapidly - cyanosis; wheezing; stridor; cool, clammy peripheries; coughing copious amounts frothy sputum with SaO2 of < 90%. Chest Xray revealed pulmonary oedema. High flow oxygen administered with little improvement in SaO2. Intubated using thiopentone 50 mg, suxamethonium 10 mg, and mechanically ventilated with 10 cm. water positive end expiratory pressure. Sedated using morphine infusion 20 mcg/ kg/ hour. Following premedication with promethazine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/ kg. and hydrocortisone 100 mg, the infant had 4 ampoules of antivenom - incrementally administered I/ V over 60 minutes. Pressure immobilization bandage removed and replaced several times over this hour, with patient undergoing rapid clinical deterioration in circulatory status with tachycardia; elevation in blood pressure; poor perfusion; cold clammy extremities on each occasion it was removed. Initial blood gas evaluation post intubation: pH - 7.19; PaCO2 - 45; PaO2 - 360. Infant paralyzed using pancuronium and given 2 X rapid infusions 5% albumin 20 ml./ kg to total of 40 ml./ kg. Pressure immobilisation bandage remained in situ; further dose of antivenom with 100 mg. hydrocortisone administered during transfer to tertiary children's hospital intensive care unit - arriving there 80 minutes post bite. She was paralyzed and ventilated with pressures of 28/ 10 cm. water and fraction of inspired oxygen of 1.0. Removal of pressure immobilization bandage again attempted - clinical deterioration in circulatory status occurred, and further bolus 20 ml/ kg plasma administered along with further ampoule antivenom and 100 mg. of hydrocortisone. Additionally required infusion sodium bicarbonate 2 mg/ kg. over 1 hour to correct persisting metabolic acidosis. Subsequently, blood pressure and pulse became normal, and 24 hours later baby was breathing spontaneously without persisting signs of envenomation. Discharged 2 days after admission to tertiary intensive care unit. At follow-up - entirely normal without untoward sequelae.

Fisher M. McD., Carr G. A., McGuiness R., and Warden J. C. (1980) Atrax Robustus Envenomation. Anaesth. Intens. Care. Vol. 8. No. 4, pp 411- 420.

Case Report.
23 yr. old previously healthy male, sustained bites X 2 to (L) knee by a male Atrax robustus while rock-climbing. Arterial tourniquet immediately applied above bite site. Spider killed and kept for identification. Assisted to Royal North Shore Hospital by companions. On arrival, 30 minutes post bite: burning pain on inside (L) thigh extending to groin; circumoral parasthesia; spasms of tongue and palate; salivation; blurred vision. Vomited X 2; complained of increasing dyspnoea; blood pressure -
160/ 100 mm.Hg; pulse - 120 b.p.m; (L) pupil fixed and dilated; spasm and rigidity of proximal and distal muscles in both upper and lower limbs. Given atropine 0.6 mg and diazepam 5mg intravenously and a further 5 mg. diazepam - transferred to intensive care unit. Chest Xray revealed diffuse interstitial pulmonary oedema; normal cardiac shadow. Blood gases (on room air): PaO2 - 56 mm.Hg;
PaCO2 - 22 mm.Hg; pH - 7.37; Hb - 17.2g/ 100 ml. Tourniquet released; oxygen administered with Hudson non-breathing mask on 12L/ min. Deteriorated rapidly, developing increasing dyspnoea; gross peripheral vascular shutdown and cyanosis; blood pressure rose to 210/ 120 mm.Hg. No response to further increments totalling 45 mg diazepam I/ V; ventilation assisted with a Mapleson D breathing circuit with 100% oxygen. Given suxamethonium 100 mg. As muscle relaxation occurred, vast quantities of pink frothy oedema fluid poured from his mouth, on to the floor, making endotracheal intubation extremely difficult. Paralyzed and commenced on IPPV with 100% oxygen, tidal volume of 1L and rate of 14 breaths / min. Following institution of ventilation a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) applied and rapidly increased until fluid was absent from tubing. The PEEP level necessary was 20 cm/ H2O. Given methylprednisolone 2g and frusemide 40 mg. There was no diuresis. His (R) pupil became fixed and dilated. Central venous catheter inserted - CVP, off respirator - 25 cm/ H20. On each occasion patient disconnected from ventilator or the PEEP reduced - copious pink frothy fluid poured into the respirator tubing. Analysis of pulmonary oedema fluid, 4 hrs. post admission, showed high levels of protein. When ventilation stabilized, blood showed PaO2 - 346 mm.Hg; PaCO2 - 68 mm.Hg; pH - 7.1. The minute volume was increased to 22L over a period to bring PaCO2 to normal levels and correct acidosis. After 90 min. blood pressure began to fall and Pa02 on 100% oxygen fell to 117mm.Hg.
Treated with infusion 25% albumin 500 ml. over 1 hour - reduced the Hb concentration to 16.2g/ 100ml. Over next 4 hrs. given 500 ml. SPPS and further 200 ml. of 25% albumin. Vasoconstriction was not improved by I/ V chlorpromazine 25 mg. - isoprenaline infusion commenced at the same time as the albumin infusion. Pulse slowed and peripheral perfusion improved over ~ 30 min.
8 hours post intubation - extubated and commenced salt and water restriction and intermittent frusemide to produce a negative salt and water balance. Radiological appearance and alveolar- arterial gradient deteriorated markedly on extubation but over next few days progressively returned to normal. Episodes of high fever over next 5 days. Complement levels and clotting screen were normal; CPK and fibrin degradation products were minimally raised. Discharged 13 days after admission.

Case Report.
Fit 40 yr. old woman, sustained bite to distal phalanx (L) index finger by a male Atrax robustus. (Positively identified) Spider had to be prised off finger; wound bled profusely. Arterial tourniquet applied - taken to Woy Woy District Hospital. Tourniquet released with no untoward effects - transferred to Gosford Hospital. On arrival, 40 min. post bite: perioral tingling; anxiety; nausea; pulse - 120 b.p.m. and over next 30 min. fell to 34 b.p.m. with blood pressure 190/ 110 mm.Hg.
ECG at this time showed blocked atrial escape which reverted to bi-directional tachycardia after atropine 0.6 mg. I/ V. Over following 2 hours: progressively more hypertensive; flushed; (L) pupil fixed and dilated; eyes puffy; developed marked peripheral vasoconstriction. Given I/ V diazepam 10 mg with no noticeable effect - transferred to ICU. Chest clear. 3 hrs. 30 min. post bite: dyspnoeic; generalised crepitations over all lung fields; blood pressure - 170/ 110 mm.Hg; pulse - 130 b.p.m; chest Xray revealed bilateral interstitial and alveolar oedema; blood gases (on room air) - PaO2 - 46 mm.Hg; PaCO2 - 28 mm.Hg; pH - 7.3. Progressively more breathless. 4 hours post bite: developed minor muscle spasms; cyanosis and gross vasoconstriction. Given: diazepam 20 mg; atropine 0.6 mg; suxamethonium 100 mg. Endotracheal tube inserted with difficulty, due to profuse pulmonary oedema which poured on to bed and floor. Commenced on IPPV, controlled with pancuronium and diazepam. PEEP applied until airway flooding ceased at 10 cm. Hb - 16.2g/ 100 ml; CVP - 16 cm.H20; protein l in serum and oedema. Rapidly developed hypotension - treated with albumin infusion and isoprenaline infusion. As blood pressure improved, peripheral vasoconstriction decreased.
Given hydrocortisone 2g; albumin infusion continued for episodes of hypotension. Over 24 hours - received further 600 ml. albumin and an increase in PEEP to 20 cm. required to maintain oxygenation.
Over next 24 hrs: became oliguric - given 500 ml. Ringer's lactate - immediately developed profuse airway flooding in spite of high levels of PEEP. This ceased within minutes of stopping infusion. Given 2 doses frusemide 80 mg. with little response. 48 hours post admission - transferred to Royal North Shore Hospital.
On arrival: stabilised on Servo volume-cycled ventilator delivering 80% oxygen with 20 cm. PEEP and minute volume 10 litres. Arterial blood gases: PO2 - 110mm.Hg; PCO2 - 50 mm.Hg; pH - 7.42. Swan-Ganz catheter inserted and pressures recorded: pulmonary artery - 40/ 26 mm.Hg; mean pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) - 23 mm.Hg; CVP - 26 cm. H2O. Reduction of PEEP led to immediate airway frothing. Given frusemide 250 mg. and methylprednisolone 2 g. X 6 hrly for 24 hrs. 1000 ml blood removed by phlebotomy over 2 hours, bringing mean PCWP to 17 mm.Hg. Diuresis began and she passed in excess of 40 ml./ hour over following 16 hours. Given 500 ml. packed cells over 4 hours to restore haematocrit. 24 hours after arrival: on 20 cm. PEEP ; PCWP (mean) -13mm.Hg; blood gases on FiO2 0.45: PaO2 - 101 mm.Hg; PaCO2 - 37 mm.Hg; pH - 7.47. 6 hrs. after admission developed high fever which persisted 48 hrs. Blood cultures negative. She became oliguric; unresponsive to increasing dosage of frusemide; serum creatinine - 0.31 mmol/ L. Given: 500 ml. fresh frozen plasma - mean PCWP increased to 17 mm.Hg. and was associated with a brisk diuresis. Continued on salt and water restriction and artificial ventilation. On 4th day: reduction of PEEP was not followed by airway frothing; commenced on intermittent mandatory ventilation; isoprenaline ceased.
On day 5: extubated - radiological deterioration of lung function after extubation.
On day 6: serum creatinine - normal; commenced on light diet. Fluid intake was gradually increased. Extremely weak for 5 days; gradually mobilized over the next week. Well on discharge 20 days post bite.
Clotting screen and complement levels were normal throughout the illness; CPK and liver function tests were marginally raised.

Sutherland S.K. (1992) Antivenom use in Australia. Premedication, adverse reactions and the use of venom detection kits. The Medical Journal of Australia, Vol. 157. pp 734-739.

Case 1.
In January 1990, a healthy 35 yr. old male from Newcastle area sustained bite to (L) toe from a male Atrax robustus - spider was in his sandshoe. Bite produced excruciating pain (felt as if toe had been cut off with a piece of glass). Arterial tourniquet applied.
2 hours 30 minutes post bite: blood pressure - 220/130 mm.Hg; pulse - 130 b.p.m; severe headache; inspiratory stridor; excessive salivation; sweating; piloerection; generalised fine fasciculations.
Given: I/ V hydrocortisone; I/ V promethazine; 1 ampoule Funnel-web spider antivenom. Headache temporarily resolved but returned in 5 minutes - given 2nd ampoule antivenom. 1 hour later: due to continuing cough and pink, frothy sputum given 3rd ampoule antivenom - dyspnoea resolved. Residual parasthesiae; tongue fasciculation; fever of 38°C still present on following morning.

Hartman L.H., Sutherland S.K.(1984) Funnel-web spider (Atrax robustus) antivenom in the treatment of human envenomation. The Medical Journal of Aust.,December 8/22. pp 796-799.

Case 1.
49 yr. old male sustained a bite to sole of (R) foot from a male Atrax robustus.
Within 5 minutes: severe local pain; sweating; piloerection; perioral tingling; palpitations; pulse - 100 b.p.m. 5 minutes later: muscle fasciculations, progressing to severe muscle spasm; vomiting; marked salivation and lachrimation. 40 minutes post bite: blood pressure - 240/ 140 mm.Hg. Given atropine and diazepam - condition unchanged - transferred to a large municipal hospital.
90 minutes post bite: given 1st dose of Funnel -web spider antivenom - no improvement - given 2nd dose antivenom 15 minutes later. Patient's condition improved over the next hour. Patient suffered from weakness and bouts of perspiration for 3 weeks post bite, although he was discharged from hospital after 2 days and resumed work after 1 week.
This case, the first in which the antivenom was administered, was a dramatic demonstration of the conversion of an illness which usually caused either death, or a hazardous course involving a hospital stay of 2 to 3 weeks, into an illness which allowed the patient to be discharged from hospital within 2 days.

Case 2.
3 yr. old boy sustained bite to (L) big toe from an Atrax robustus. Arterial tourniquet applied; signs of envenomation not apparent until tourniquet removal 1 hour post bite.
Within 4 minutes: acutely distressed; copious salivation; lachrimation; sweating; piloerection. 5 minutes later: profuse, fluffy, straw-coloured pulmonary fluid was emerging from mouth; cyanosed; disorientated. Hyperthermia and opisthotonus - signs which had not been described previously in Atrax robustus envenomation - occurred; these may have been caused by the administration either of cold stable plasma protein solution (SPPS) or of promethazine. Venous access was difficult, and 30 minutes elapsed form onset of severe symptoms to administration of antivenom. Recovery was slow over several hours - it is considered in retrospect that a further dose of antivenom may have accelerated the rate of recovery. Patient discharged after 2 days in hospital - on later follow-up showed no sequelae of disease or as a result of treatment.

Case 5.
60 yr. old male, sustained bite to (R) ring finger from a male Atrax robustus. History of rheumatoid arthritis - taking naproxen and dextropropoxyphene tablets. Ambulance officers applied a venous tourniquet, splint, bandaged the arm. On removal of tourniquet in hospital, 2 hours later: profuse sweating; lachrimation; salivation; perioral parasthesia. Antivenom was administered 90 minutes after tourniquet's removal. Recovery satisfactory - patient discharged from hospital next day.
4 days post discharge: returned to casualty department with headache; nausea; backache and dark bowel motions. No signs of malaena detected. Results of haematological and biochemical investigations and Xrays were normal. Patient sent home.
3 days later: returned to casualty department with headache; nausea; had some signs of meningismus. Patient admitted for observation. Medical officer concluded that there was no connection between the
envenomation and patient's subsequent hospital visits.

Case 6.
82 yr. old male, sustained bite (R) palm from a male Atrax robustus. History of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus - diet controlled; complete heart block - permanent pacemaker in situ and taking frusemide, potassium chloride, isosorbide dinitrate. Although a constrictive bandage was applied by ambulance officers, severe pain, sweating and hypertension were noted during transport. On arrival at hospital, he also had leg muscle cramps, salivation and periorbital fasciculation. Antivenom was administered promptly, and the signs and symptoms of envenomation resolved rapidly. He was discharged from hospital 2 days after admission.

Case 9.
70 yr. old woman sustained bite to (R) index finger by a male Atrax robustus. Immediately bandaged finger and signs of envenomation did not appear until bandage was removed in hospital, one hour later. She had local pain, profuse sweating, blurred vision and tingling around the mouth. A lymphatic tourniquet was applied, and she was transferred to a major municipal hospital.
2 hours post bite: profuse sweating; piloerection; fasciculation of the tongue; blood pressure - 210/ 100 mm.Hg.
3 hours post bite: given antivenom - within 20 minutes all signs and symptoms, except sweating, had subsided. Sweating continued for a further hour. Patient discharged from hospital next day.

Torda T.A.,Loong E.,Greaves I.(1980)Severe Lung Oedema and Fatal Consumption Coagulopathy After Funnel-Web Bite. The Medical Journal of Aust. Oct 18. pp 442- 444.

Case Report.
Previously healthy 31 yr. o ld female, sustained bite to wrist from a male Atrax robustus. Immediately applied tourniquet. 30 minutes post bite: blurred vision; sweating; sense of increasing anxiety. On admission to hospital, 45 min post bite: pulse - 76 b.p.m; blood pressure -170/ 105mm.Hg
Within 10 minutes: muscular twitching; generalized muscle spasms; profuse salivation; nausea; vomiting; respiratory difficulty. Over next 90 minutes: given atropine 600mcg; diazepam 40 mg; frusemide 40 mg; promethazine 25 mg. While receiving oxygen at 6L/ min via Hudson mask, arterial blood gas analysis showed: pH - 7.29; PaCO2 - 24 mm.Hg; PaO2 - 46 mm.Hg; base deficit - 14 mmol/ L.
3 hours post bite: stuporous; irritable; cyanosed; tachypnoeic (28/ min); generalized muscular spasms; tachycardia of 180 b.p.m with frequent ventricular ectopic beats; blood pressure - 160/ 110 mm.Hg.
After intravenous administration of alcuronium 20 mg, nasotracheal tube inserted, and a positive pressure ventilation with 100% oxygen and an end - expiratory pressure of 5 cmH2O was instituted. Arterial blood gases showed: pH - 7.27; PaCO2 - 33 mm.Hg; PaO2 - 91 mm.Hg. Laryngoscopy revealed pink frothy fluid issuing from larynx. Chest Xray showed "gross alveolar pulmonary oedema involving almost the entire (R) lung. There is also some interstitial oedema in (L) lung. Heart size is normal." An earlier chest Xray taken on admission, showed no abnormalities. Patient's condition remained stable for next 4 hours. Morphine was administered intravenously to facilitate controlled ventilation, and increments of pancuronium were also occasionally necessary. 5 - 7 hours post bite: blood pressure unrecordable; urine output ceased; pupils dilated, reacting sluggishly to light; sinus tachycardia - 180 b.p.m persisted.
Given: rapid infusion 1.5 litres S.P.P.S; dopamine infusion of 10mcg/ kg per minute; I/ V digoxin 0.5 mg. Condition improved. 11 hrs. post bite: systolic blood pressure - 80mm.Hg. - 100 mm.Hg; urine output recommenced; pupils constricted and became reactive. On following morning: alert; able to understand verbal reassurance. Pulmonary function continued to deteriorate as did Xray picture. Falling arterial oxygen tension required increase of positive end expiratory pressure to 10 cm. H2O. Administration of 200 ml. concentrated albumin produced no improvement. Transferred to The Prince Henry Hospital, Sydney.
On arrival: paralyzed but conscious; blood [reassure - 90/ 60 mm.Hg; pulse - 148 b.p.m. while receiving dopamine at rate of 20 mcg/ kg per minute. With positive end expiratory pressure of 10 cm.H2O, arterial blood gases: pH - 7.37; PaCO2 - 38 mm.Hg; PaO2 - 61 mm.Hg. Swan-Ganz catheter introduced. Chest Xray showed pulmonary oedema without cardiomegaly, suggestive of the "adult respiratory distress syndrome". Temperature varied between 38.5°C and 40°C. Given: gentamycin 60 mg and dexamethasone 120 mg. Ventilation continued with oxygen and the end expiratory pressure was increased to 15 cm. H2O. During the night the PaO2 gradually decreased to 53 mm.Hg. despite an increase in PEEP to 18 cm.H2O. On the following morning (day 3 post bite): surgical emphysema present in neck; chest Xray showed presence of pneumomediastinum. After repeated haemodynamic measurements, PEEP was reduced to 15 cm.H2O. Later the same day, (R) forearm and both feet became cool and cyanosed. Although conscious, by early evening patient could no longer move her (R) arm or leg on command; hyperreflexia and poorly sustained clonus were noted on that side. Haemoglobin from 146g/ L to 105g/ L; prothrombin index - 42%; partial thromboplastin time - 75s. Blood film demonstrated "low-normal" platelet count. Concentrations of electrolytes, calcium, phosphate and total proteins were within normal limits. Plasma bilirubin level - 34 micromol/ L; serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) - 570u; serum urea - 15 micromol/ L; serum creatinine - 0.13 mmol/ L.
4 days post bite: further clinical deterioration; unconscious; (R) side flaccid. EEG showed symmetrical 1Hz to 5Hz activity, which by the afternoon, was interrupted by occasional periods of isovoltage lasting about 1 second. Respiratory status remained stable; blood pressure - 85/ 50 mm.Hg to 100/ 60 mm.Hg - required a continuous dopamine infusion of 25 mcg./ kg per min. Despite presence of peripheral pulses, (R) arm and legs to knees were cyanosed. By afternoon, 3 fingers of (L) hand had also become dusky; slight haematuria; bleeding time - 7 minutes; Pl - 54%; PTTK - 51s; platelet count - 53 X 10 exp.9/ L; FDP - 40 mcg/ ml. These results suggested consumption coagulopathy. Treatment was begun with the administration of heparin 5000 u followed by 2000 u every 4 hours; 2 units fresh frozen plasma. Haemoglobin level - 115g/ L and results of biochemical tests had not changed significantly from those on previous day, except for a further rise in the ALT to 990 u.
On morning of 5th day: arterial blood gases showed metabolic acidaemia, base deficit of 10 mmol/ L which was corrected with 100 mmol of sodium bicarbonate. Through latter part of day, circulation and ventilation remained stable but heart rate was 150 b.p.m. All 4 limbs were deeply cyanosed; barely responding to painful stimuli on (L) side; unresponsive and flaccid on (R). Both fundi showed early papilloedema; EEG showed frequent 2-s periods of silence interrupting slow (1Hz to 5Hz) activity.
Temperature varied up to 41°C and did not respond to aspirin, paracetamol, fanning or sponging. Patient began bleeding from rectum and vagina as well as from previous puncture sites. Microscopic haematuria continued. Haemoglobin - 100g/ L; Pl - 42%; PTTK - 88s; platelet count - 28 X 10 exp.9/ L;
FDP - 50mcg/ ml. Treatment with heparin and fresh frozen plasma continued; plasma concentrate not available. Later, in evening: bleeding from nose and mouth. 2 further units of fresh frozen plasma and 2 units of 4 day old whole blood were given through the night. Although serum electrolyte levels remained normal, serum creatinine level had risen to 0.23 mmol/ L by that morning. Later, urine output fell below 30 / hr, despite a blood pressure higher than 90 mm.Hg systolic. By 0215 hrs. day 6: patient virtually anuric and remained unresponsive to the administration of frusemide 120 mg; cardiac output was 3.4L/ minute. At 0700 hrs: blood gases showed metabolic acidaemia (12 mmol/ L) which was again corrected with 100ml. of sodium bicarbonate solution. About 1100 hrs: blood pressure fell to 60/ 40 mm.Hg, and pulse rate decreased from 150 to 120 beats per minute. An increased infusion of dopamine had no effect. Patient died in asystole at 1200 hrs - just over 6 days post bite.

## Clinical Effects

Fatal outcome common in untreated severe cases

Funnel web spiders have a low rate of effective bites, but when systemic envenoming does occur it is often very rapid in onset, with tingling of the lips or tongue, followed by tongue fasciculation within 10-30 minutes. There is then rapid progression, with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, piloerection, hypersalivation, hyperlachrymation, increased sweating, anxiety and development of often severe pulmonary oedema, with hypoxia and coma. Convulsions, though not common, may occur. Untreated, this progression may result in death in 1-2 hours (shortest time 15 minutes), or longer in adults. If this early phase is not lethal, the patient may show subsidence of the symptoms, followed by muscle fasciculations, progressive hypotension and cardiac failure or arrest. Death is a result of either fulminant pulmonary oedema or intractable hypotension and cardiac arrest. At least 13 deaths are recorded for this species.

### Special Risk Groups
#### Children

Risk to children is similar to risk for adults, but childs smaller body mass implies comparative venom concentration will be higher, so more severe envenoming likely, the increased risk being inversely proportional to the child's size.

#### Pregnancy

Potential risk to foetus from systemic envenoming, similar to risk to mother

#### Elderly

The higher incidence of pre-existing diseases in the elderly and associated frailty place them at higher risk. Increased risk will largely be determined by nature and extent of pre-existing disease and by any medications used to treat such disease.

### Specific Effects Relating to Body Systems or Venom Types

Rare, usually secondary

#### Coagulopathy

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### System Effects

Headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, coma, rarely convulsions.

#### Local Effects

Local pain only

Bite marks obvious from large fangs, with local pain, but usually no other local reaction.

#### Necrosis

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Myotoxicity

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Neurotoxic Paralysis

#### Renal Damage

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Untreated Lethality

Most cases minor, but in severe cases, high lethality rate if untreated.

#### Venom Anticoagulants

Not present

#### Venom Cardiotoxins

Secondary cardiotoxicity only

#### Venom Haemorrhagins

Not present

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Venom Myotoxins

Not present

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

Not present

Not present

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Venom Neurotoxins

Excitatory neurotoxins

Possibility of neuro-excitatory envenoming, described as a "catecholamine storm", with tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary oedema, piloerection, muscle fasciculation, increased sweating, salivation.

Not present

No other clinically important effects are noted

## Description

### Adult Length

No Data

No data

### Coloration & Markings

Glossy dark brown to black on the carapace and brown to black, often with a plum tinge, on the dorsolateral abdomen.

### Habits

Terrestrial predator. Tends to construct its retreat on the ground beneath rocks and fallen timber, often on gully slopes with moist soil. The white silk tube is long, sometimes up to 0.6 metres with a Y- or T-shaped entrance offerring two points of entry or exit and braced with many struts to hold it in position.

### Prey

Feeds mainly on insects, their larvae, snails, millipedes, skinks frogs or any other small creature wandering near the retreat entrance.

### Taxonomy Synonomy

Atrax robustus, Cambridge, 1877.
Atrax robustus, Hogg, 1901.
Euctimena tibialis, Rainbow, 1914.
Poikilomorpha montana, Rainbow, 1914.
Atrax robustus, Main, 1964; Nishikawa, 1976; Gray, 1984; Gray, 1988.

## Diagnosis

Painful bite, rapid development of systemic envenoming, with perioral tingling, tongue fasciculation, headache, nausea, increased sweating, salivation, lachrymation, piloerection, hypertension, pulmonary oedema.

### Likely Effects
- Direct Cardiotoxin Effect
- Excitatory Neurotoxicity
- Localised Effects at bite/string/contact location
- Respiratory Effects
- Non-specific General System Effects
### Possible Effects
- Effects on Red Blood Cells (potentially including haemolysis)
- Effects on White Blood Cells (notably Leukocytosis and/or Lymphopenia)
- Effects on Platelets (increase, decrease, change in platelet aggregation)
- Myotoxic (local or systemic muscle damage)
- Dermatological Effects
- Cardiovascular Effects
- Angio Oedema or Major Allergic Reaction
- Other
- Renal Effects (primary or secondary)
### Effects Unlikely to be observed
- Abnormal Haemostasis and Bleeding
- Paralytic Neurotoxicity
- Primary Necrotoxicity at bite/sting/contact location
- Venom Spit Ophthalmia
- Anterior Pituitary Haemorrhage

## First Aid

Keep victim still, apply pressure immobilisation bandage & splint, gently wash bite area, transport to medical care

First aid for Funnel Web Spider Bites (Australia)

1. If the spider is still attached, immediately remove it, being careful not to sustain further bites, and place to spider in a jam jar or other container, so it may be brought to the hospital for identification.
1. After ensuring the patient and onlookers are no longer at risk of further bites by the spider, the bitten person should be reassured and persuaded to lie down and remain still. Many will be terrified, fearing sudden death and, in this mood, they may behave irrationally or even hysterically. The basis for reassurance is the fact that many bites do not result in envenoming, and the effectiveness of modern medical treatment.
1. The bite wound should not be tampered with in any way.
1. If the bite is on a limb, a broad bandage (even torn strips of clothing or pantyhose) should be applied over the bitten area at moderate pressure (as for a sprain; not so tight circulation is impaired), then extended to cover as much of the bitten limb as possible, including fingers or toes, going over the top of clothing rather than risking excessive limb movement by removing clothing. The bitten limb should then be immobilised as effectively as possible using an extemporised splint or sling.
1. If there is any impairment of vital functions, such as problems with respiration, airway, circulation, heart function, these must be supported as a priority. In particular, both airway and respiration may be impaired, requiring urgent and prolonged treatment, which may include the mouth to mask (mouth to mouth) technique of expired air transfer. Seek urgent medical attention.
1. Do not use Tourniquets, cut, suck or scarify the wound or apply chemicals or electric shock.
1. Avoid peroral intake, absolutely no alcohol. No sedatives outside hospital. If there will be considerable delay before reaching medical aid, measured in several hours to days, then give clear fluids by mouth to prevent dehydration.
1. If the offending spider has been killed or caught it should be brought with the patient for identification. Many relatively harmless spiders may appear similar to the funnel web spiders and there are several species of funnel web spiders, so identification of the spider is important.
1. The spider bite victim should be transported as quickly and as passively as possible to the nearest place where they can be seen by a medically-trained person (health station, dispensary, clinic or hospital). The bitten limb must not be exercised as muscular contraction will promote systemic absorption of venom. If no motor vehicle or boat is available, the patient can be carried on a stretcher or hurdle, on the pillion or crossbar of a bicycle or on someone's back.
1. Most traditional, and many of the more recently fashionable, first aid measures are useless and potentially dangerous. These include local cauterization, incision, excision, amputation, suction by mouth, vacuum pump or syringe, combined incision and suction ("venom-ex" apparatus), injection or instillation of compounds such as potassium permanganate, phenol (carbolic soap) and trypsin, application of electric shocks or ice (cryotherapy), use of traditional herbal, folk and other remedies including the ingestion of emetic plant products and parts of the snake, multiple incisions, tattooing and so on.

## Medical Treatment

Funnel web spider bites, though mostly minor, can cause severe, even fatal envenoming rapidly, so all cases should be managed as a medical emergency. At the first sign of systemic envenoming, IV CSL Funnel Web Spider Antivenom should be given, 2-4 vials initially, depending on severity, followed by further doses if envenoming persists or recurs.

Most cases of funnel web spider bite will not show systemic envenoming and will not require antivenom. While systemic envenoming usually develops rapidly, occasionally it is delayed. All suspected funnel web spider bites should be observed in hospital for at least 8hrs, or overnight for children. First aid should be left on for 3-4hrs as this may assist local inactivation of venom. Systemic envenoming by funnel web spiders is a medical emergency requiring urgent IV antivenom therapy. At the earliest sign of systemic envenoming, such as perioral tingling or tongue fasciculation, give antivenom. The initial dose should be 2 vials CSL Funnel Web Spider Antivenom (4 vials if major envenoming already present), but be prepared to give further doses. 6-8 vials is common for severe envenoming. Higher doses have occasionally been required. Continued pulmonary oedema requires further antivenom (unless it is certain the oedema is purely due to iatrogenic IV fluid overload). Relapse requires further antivenom. As late relapse can occur, any patient requiring antivenom must be admitted and observed for at least 24hrs.

### Management in Detail
#### Immediate Effects Management

Establish IV line, IV fluids, secure airway, maintain respiration if imperiled, treat hypotension (if present), clean wound

#### Approach to Management

All cases should be treated as urgent & potentially lethal. Rapid assessment & commencement of treatment including appropriate antivenom (if indicated & available) is mandatory. Admit all cases.

#### Follow Up

Follow up all cases given antivenom therapy, checking particularly for serum sickness

#### Local Effects Management

Clean wound

#### Systemic Effects Management

Symptomatic care + IV fluids (as required)

#### Cardiotoxin Effects Management

No primary cardiotoxicity, but monitor for secondary arrhythmias, treat with antivenom.

#### Haematologic Effects Management

Haematologic effects not likely

#### Haematologic Other Effects Management

Not applicable

#### Important Laboratory Test

Laboratory tests unhelpful in management.

#### Myotoxic Effects Management

Myotoxicity not likely

#### Necrotoxin Effects Management

Local necrosis unlikely

#### Neurotoxic Excitatory Effects Management

Support respiration, protect airway, intubate & ventilate if required for severe pulmonary oedema, give appropriate antivenom at earliest sign of systemic envenoming.

#### Other Neurotoxic Effects Management

Not applicable

#### Neurotoxic Paralytic Effects Management

Paralytic effects not likely

#### Other Issues in Treatment

If severe pulmonary oedema develops, and sufficient antivenom is not available, intubate & give positive pressure ventilation.

#### Other Specific Effects Management

Ensure tetanus immunisation

#### Renal Effects Management

Renal damage unlikely

## Venom

### Venom Components

- Robustoxin [ Syn : RBX ] Polypeptide Neurotoxin. Sodium Channel Blocker. Sheumack et al (1983) ( Ref : R001108 ).
- Average Venom Quantity

0.14 mg ( dry weight ), Sutherland and Tibballs (2001) ( Ref : R001112 ).

### Neurotoxins Channel Toxins

Robustoxin : Isolated and N-terminal sequence determined ( first 27 AA residues ) by Sheumack et al (1983) ( Ref : R001108 ) and fully sequenced by Sheumack et al (1985) ( Ref : R001110 ). Robustoxin is a polypeptide of 42 AA residues cross-linked by 4 disulfide bonds, high in Lys and deficient in Val and His and with a Mol. Wt. approx 5,800. Robustoxin is a Na+ channel blocker. Evidence suggests that robustoxin adopts the inhibitor cystine knot structure. Temple et al (1999) ( Ref : R001109 ) and Craik et al (2001) ( Ref : R001111 ).

### Component ld50

Robustoxin : 0.16 mg / kg sc ( newborn mice ), Sheumack et al (1983) ( Ref : R001108 ).
